Other triggers and strategies center on emergency/police/location cues, while no threat, appraisal, or memory content connects to animals or snakes. This makes that item look clinically disconnected rather than merely unusual.

issues.explanation: Compulsive cleaning can occur after sexual assault, but in this profile it is not supported by the other selected items or the formulation. The active pattern strongly links triggers, threat, and negative appraisals to maladaptive strategies, yet the listed triggers/threats/appraisals point to hypervigilance, emergency/uniform cues, and situational avoidance rather than contamination, dirtiness, or washing/control themes. As selected here, the cleaning item appears insufficiently connected to the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Tariq, a 54-year-old software engineer, had always prided himself on his logical mind and meticulous approach to life, but for the past several years, his world had felt anything but logical. It began after an incident in his late forties, a sexual assault that occurred late one evening in the deserted office building of a previous job. He had been working alone, focused on a complex coding problem, when a male security guard, someone he had seen around but never properly interacted with, entered his office. The memory of that night was a visceral, unwelcome guest in his mind, particularly the distant wail of sirens that had seemed to mock his helplessness as the assault unfolded. He had come to believe that what happened to him was deeply unfair and that nothing had been done to truly address it, a bitter resentment that festered alongside a quiet, gnawing certainty that the event had happened because of the way he acted, a belief that haunted his waking hours.

Now, years later, Tariq’s life was a carefully constructed fortress of avoidance. The sound of a siren, whether from an ambulance screaming down the street outside his apartment or a police car passing his vehicle on the freeway, was a physical jolt, sending a surge of adrenaline through him. His heart would race, his palms would sweat, and he would often react as if he were in immediate danger, even when he knew, intellectually, that nothing was actually wrong. This constant state of alert meant he was always scanning his surroundings for signs of danger, his eyes darting to every corner of a room, every face in a crowd. He found himself most comfortable only in a very limited number of places—his apartment, certain aisles of his regular grocery store, and his cubicle at work, provided no one else was too close.

His fear of being alone with men had subtly reshaped his social landscape, which, as a single man, had already been somewhat limited. He turned down invitations from male colleagues for lunch or after-work drinks, fabricating excuses about deadlines or prior engagements. He avoided the gym during peak hours, preferring to go late at night when fewer men were present. The sight of military or police uniforms, even on television, would make him visibly tense. In his daily life, this translated into an intense aversion to authority figures. He would go to great lengths to avoid interaction with the building security guards at his current software firm, taking the stairs rather than risking a shared elevator ride, or waiting until he saw them leave a communal area before entering himself. He would cross the street if he saw a police officer, his body tightening with a nameless dread.

He had also completely cut off any path that would take him near the old office building where the assault occurred, even if it meant adding significant time to his commute. This avoidance, over weeks and months, had gradually shrunk his world. His once vibrant curiosity had dulled; he rarely explored new places or met new people. He found himself increasingly isolated, and with that isolation came a profound sense of emptiness. He had come to believe he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, that the capacity for joy, connection, or even simple contentment had been irrevocably stolen from him. The exhaustion of constant vigilance, the effort required to maintain his intricate web of avoidance, had become overwhelming. He was tired of the relentless scanning for danger, tired of the false alarms that left him trembling, tired of the shrinking confines of his safe zones. It was this profound weariness, coupled with a flicker of hope that perhaps he didn’t have to live this way forever, that finally led Tariq to seek help, though he wasn’t entirely sure what he was hoping for, beyond a quiet cessation of the fear that had defined his life for so long.
